blocks.text: A file operation has at least three outcomes to distinguish: acquiring the handle, completing the requested work, and releasing the handle. Successfully opening a file proves only the first. Writing can fail later, and a buffered output error can become visible during an explicit completion step. RAII makes cleanup reliable along ordinary control-flow paths; it does not make every operation on the resource succeed.

topics.title: 3.1 Understanding Resources Beyond Memory
topics.summary: A resource is something whose acquisition creates a corresponding obligation: release a file, unlock a mutex, return a buffer, or close a native handle. Memory is only one example. Ownership must identify which object performs that release and whether responsibility can be copied or transferred.

blocks.text: Think of a resource as something with a finite lifetime and a release obligation. Memory is one example. A file, mutex lock, transaction reservation, device context, or operating-system handle can have the same shape: acquire, use, release. The details of the release function differ, but the design question remains who is responsible for invoking it exactly once for each successful acquisition.

blocks.text: A resource may be scarce even when its C++ representation is small. An integer descriptor can refer to an open file in the operating system. Copying that integer does not necessarily create an independently releasable resource. Deleting an integer object does not close the descriptor. This is why ownership cannot be inferred from the number of bytes in a handle or from whether its representation is a pointer.

blocks.text: Some acquisitions are logically paired with a different completion operation. Holding a lock requires unlocking; beginning a transaction may require commit or rollback; opening an output stream may require checking a flush or close result. Define the fallback behavior first. If ordinary work throws before completion, what should destruction do? A rollback-like fallback is often appropriate for an uncommitted transaction, while a file wrapper normally attempts release without claiming that data is durable.

Encapsulate the native mechanism locally, then expose an interface that states its actual guarantees.

Separate resource release, successful output completion, and durability requirements. A file destructor closing a stream is not a substitute for a reviewed persistence protocol.

blocks.text: Object lifetime supplies a structured cleanup boundary. A fully constructed automatic object is destroyed when its scope exits normally and during ordinary exception unwinding. Its members are destroyed according to the language’s lifetime rules. By placing the release obligation inside that object, the cleanup follows all those exits without a separate cleanup label at each return statement.
rich: Object lifetime supplies a structured cleanup boundary. A fully constructed automatic object is destroyed when its scope exits normally and during ordinary exception unwinding. Its members are destroyed according to the language’s lifetime rules. By placing the release obligation inside that object, the cleanup follows all those exits without a separate cleanup label at each return statement.

blocks.text: The phrase “fully constructed” matters. If a constructor throws before finishing, the destructor of the incomplete enclosing object is not called. Members that completed construction are still cleaned up. Therefore an owning resource should be represented by a member whose own construction establishes ownership, rather than by an unprotected raw handle stored only after several other potentially failing actions. Chapter 18 of Book I introduced construction order; here that order becomes a failure-management tool.

blocks.text: RAII is not a guarantee against every termination mode. Abrupt process termination, a fatal signal, a power loss, or deliberate termination mechanisms can bypass ordinary stack unwinding. A server requiring recovery after a crash needs persistent formats and external recovery procedures in addition to C++ cleanup. Keep claims local: the example demonstrates cleanup during a controlled exception, not crash consistency or storage durability.

blocks.text: For wrappers that acquire several resources, acquire them through already-owning members or local guards. If the second acquisition fails, the first resource must not depend on the destructor of an object whose construction never completed. This is where composition provides real exception safety rather than merely a destructor-shaped promise.

blocks.text: Construction should either establish the wrapper’s stated usable state or report failure without leaving a leaked acquisition behind. The temporary-file wrapper calls its acquisition function and checks the result. Copying is prohibited because a shallow copy would give two wrappers the same apparent release obligation. blocks.text: A destructor cannot conveniently report a late write failure to a caller that has already committed success. Therefore code with a meaningful output-completion requirement should explicitly finish or close and check before reporting success. The destructor remains the fallback for failure paths. After explicit close, the raw borrowed handle returned by get() is no longer usable; the interface is intentionally narrow and its precondition must be respected.

blocks.text: A destructor is a poor place for a recoverable error conversation. The caller may already be handling another exception, and the object is ending its lifetime. Throwing another exception from cleanup can terminate execution during unwinding. A practical wrapper therefore separates explicit checked completion from fallback cleanup. The normal path calls close() and examines the result; destruction releases any remaining handle without pretending to report every possible failure.

blocks.text: Clear the stored ownership state before invoking a native release operation when that is the wrapper’s chosen one-shot policy. The example moves the old FILE* into a local variable, sets the member to null, and then calls fclose once. A second close() does nothing. This does not imply that every operating-system API has identical retry semantics. A descriptor or device wrapper must follow its own API’s documented release behavior rather than copying a file-stream pattern blindly.

A destructor cannot conveniently report a late write failure to a caller that has already committed success. Therefore code with a meaningful output-completion requirement should explicitly finish or close and check before reporting success. The destructor remains the fallback for failure paths. After explicit close, the raw borrowed handle returned by get() is no longer usable; the interface is intentionally narrow and its precondition must be respected.

A destructor is a poor place for a recoverable error conversation. The caller may already be handling another exception, and the object is ending its lifetime. Throwing another exception from cleanup can terminate execution during unwinding. A practical wrapper therefore separates explicit checked completion from fallback cleanup. The normal path calls close() and examines the result; destruction releases any remaining handle without pretending to report every possible failure.

Clear the stored ownership state before invoking a native release operation when that is the wrapper’s chosen one-shot policy. The example moves the old FILE* into a local variable, sets the member to null, and then calls fclose once. A second close() does nothing. This does not imply that every operating-system API has identical retry semantics. A descriptor or device wrapper must follow its own API’s documented release behavior rather than copying a file-stream pattern blindly.

Destructors should also avoid unrelated work that can fail. Logging into a growing vector may allocate; formatting a diagnostic string may throw. The chapter’s live-count observer modifies an integer in an enclosing scope, so its instrumentation does not require allocation. Later lifecycle examples reserve fixed observation capacity before recording destructor events. Instrumentation is part of the program and can introduce exactly the failure being investigated.

The result is a narrow but useful guarantee: along the tested ordinary paths, one successful acquisition leads to one release attempt, and exceptions do not bypass the owner’s cleanup. Claims about successful writes, durable storage, or external consistency require separate tests and policies.

topics.title: Failure clinic — The destructor that never ran
topics.summary: A novice places a raw handle in an enclosing object and expects that object’s destructor to clean it up if later constructor work throws. The expectation is wrong when the enclosing constructor never completed. The repair is not another broad catch in every caller. Put the handle into a completed RAII member or a local owner before beginning the later work, so a completed subobject has the release obligation.

topics.title: Review and solution reasoning
topics.summary: RAII addresses release responsibility. It does not guarantee that the resource was acquired, that every operation succeeded, or that external data is durable. A completed member can clean up when an enclosing constructor fails; the incomplete enclosing object’s destructor is not the fallback. An explicit completion method can surface errors while ordinary destruction supplies a nonthrowing cleanup path. These distinctions let a wrapper remain both convenient and honest about failure.
